answer_anchors.text: A bias-correcting or informative sensitivity analysis indicates the result was not biased.
The available evidence does not show that the result was free from missing-data bias.

questions.bias_construct: Whether there is evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data.
considerations: Imputation alone is not evidence that missing outcome data did not bias the result.

Availability and mitigation are separate premises: a familiar method name or numerically stable estimate is not enough; the sensitivity analysis must span plausible assumptions relevant to the documented missingness mechanism.
This question permits complete ascertainment, mechanism-matched reassurance, and legitimate uncertainty. Do not apply a universal percentage threshold in place of a Result-specific impact judgment.
questions.decision_rule: Evidence may come from methods correcting for bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions about missingness and true outcome. The assumptions must match the documented missingness mechanism and the approved Result. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship. Last-observation-carried-forward or multiple imputation based only on intervention group should not be assumed to correct bias.
evidence_needed: A bias-correcting analysis or sensitivity analysis with plausible missingness assumptions and its result, including the missingness mechanism it addresses.
If the source only changes intervention-group attribution or analysis membership, record that distinction; do not describe it as a test of unobserved outcome values without source support.
invalid_shortcuts: multiple imputation based only on intervention group
questions.no_information_rule: No_information is not an allowed response to this question in the parallel-assignment pack; provide direct evidence or answer no/probably no.
questions.official_guidance: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
questions.wording: If N/PN/NI to 3.1: Is there evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data?

answer_anchors.text: Missingness could depend on the true outcome value.
Documented missingness reasons are unrelated to the outcome.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value.
considerations: For time-to-event outcomes, inspect censoring reasons and timing to identify missing follow-up. A common administrative cutoff does not by itself establish outcome-dependent missingness.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring is not by itself evidence that observation stopped. This question asks whether the missingness mechanism could depend on the true value; it is not a question about analysis membership.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when loss to follow-up or withdrawal could relate to health status or outcome. Answer no or probably no when all missingness had documented reasons unrelated to outcome, such as a failed measuring device or interruption to routine data collection.
evidence_needed: Reasons for missingness and their relationship to participants' health status or true outcome, including censoring and treatment switching in time-to-event analyses.
invalid_shortcuts: a reason for withdrawal without its relation to outcome
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the reasons for missingness do not permit assessment of dependence on the true value.
questions.official_guidance: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
questions.wording: If N/PN to 3.2: Could missingness in the outcome depend on its true value?

answer_anchors.text: Missingness likely depended on the true outcome value.
The analysis accounted for characteristics explaining the relationship, or dependence was not likely.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness that could depend on true value likely depended on it.
considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Judge likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances; absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.
questions.decision_rule: Consider differences in missingness or censoring rates, reasons that depend on true value, reasons differing between groups, trial circumstances, and censoring after stopping or changing intervention. Answer no when analysis accounted for participant characteristics likely to explain the relationship.
evidence_needed: Group-specific missingness or censoring, reasons for missingness, trial circumstances, and any analysis accounting for relevant participant characteristics.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of dependence on true value cannot be judged from the available evidence.
questions.official_guidance: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 3.3: Is it likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value?

questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

evidence.transcription: Supplementary Figure S1, “Enrolment and Randomization of Patients for the Analysis of Overall Survival.” Among 2,751 patients randomized to the trial platform, 834 were allocated to other research arms and 1,917 entered this comparison: 957 allocated to A (SOC-only) and 960 to G (SOC+AAP). Follow-up status: A, alive with data in past year n=637, alive with no data in past year n=58, died n=262; G, alive with data in past year n=718, alive with no data in past year n=58, died n=184. Efficacy analyses included 957 A and 960 G participants. The safety analysis included 960 SOC-only reported (957 A and 11 G) and 949 immediate AAP started (949 G); analyzed safety counts were 960 (4/957 A and 11 G excluded for no AE assessment) and 948 (1/949 G excluded for no AE assessment).

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

answer_anchors.text: Measurement or ascertainment could differ between intervention groups.

questions.bias_construct: Whether measurement or ascertainment of the outcome could have differed between intervention groups.
considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.
evidence_needed: Methods, thresholds, timing, and opportunities for outcome ascertainment in each intervention group, plus the pathway connecting any opportunity difference to differential detection.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when comparability of measurement or ascertainment cannot be assessed.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome assessors were aware of the intervention received, when 4.1 and 4.2 are not yes/probably yes. Identify the assessor's identity and role: who determines the approved outcome at the relevant time point, not merely who records it.
considerations: The assessor can be a participant, intervention provider, or independent observer.

This asks only whether the relevant assessor knew assignment. It does not establish that the measurement was susceptible to bias, that detection opportunities differed, or that knowledge likely changed the assessment; those are separate questions.
Unknown assessor identity or awareness does not prevent conditional reasoning about whether the measurement could be influenced if awareness existed.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when the outcome assessor was blinded to intervention status. For participant-reported outcomes, the participant is the outcome assessor, so participant blinding can determine this answer. This question is applicable only after the stated activation conditions.
evidence_needed: Who assessed the outcome and whether that assessor was blinded to intervention status.

questions.bias_construct: Whether assessment could have been influenced by knowledge of intervention received. Keep assessor awareness separate from the mechanism by which awareness could change a judgement.
considerations: Assess whether knowledge could influence this outcome. Evidence that influence actually occurred belongs to 4.5; its absence does not resolve 4.4.

Possible influence requires a judgement or reporting pathway through which assessor awareness could matter. Awareness alone is not a measurement difference, and a susceptible outcome does not by itself show that influence was possible in this assessment.
When a composite mixes objective and subjective components, assess each component's pathway separately and retain uncertainty where a component-specific link is unresolved.
questions.decision_rule: Knowledge could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving judgement, and intervention-provider decisions; it is unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes without judgement, such as all-cause mortality. A standardized instrument does not remove judgment from elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment.

questions.bias_construct: Whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced outcome assessment. Require evidence or strong beliefs plus a judgement opportunity; awareness alone does not establish influence.
considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.
Objective components can provide valid reassurance for those components without overriding likely influence or unresolved Evidence for subjective components in the same Result.
questions.decision_rule: Distinguish possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence. Strong beliefs about benefits or harms make influence more likely, for example patient-reported symptoms or recovery assessed by an intervention provider. A standardized scale or grading rule does not by itself remove an elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment pathway.
evidence_needed: Evidence of actual influence or strong beliefs and judgement opportunities that make influence likely, given the assessor and outcome.

Abiraterone for Prostate Cancer
ards (P = 0.31) or of heterogeneity of the treat-
ment effect according to metastatic status at
randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
parisons in patients without metastatic disease
at randomization are immature, currently with
78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
groups (Fig. 2A).
Failure-free Survival
There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
survival was 75% in the combination group and
45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
the combination group and 30.0 months in the
ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
progression or death from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
80% in the combination group and 62% in the
ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
radiologic progression or death from prostate
cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
mentary Appendix). This difference was most
marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
Exploratory Analyses
Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
noted in older patients. In patients younger than
70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
there were 65 events in the combination group
and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
0.50; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.68; P = 0.10 for interac-
tion). In patients younger than 70 years of age,
there were 93 deaths from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 154 in the ADT-alone
group (subhazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39 to
0.66); in patients 70 years of age or older, there
were 47 deaths from prostate cancer in the com-
bination group and 62 in the ADT-alone group
(subhazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.17;
P = 0.08 for interaction).
Adverse Events
Patients in the safety population who reported
adverse events of grade 3 or higher during their
entire time in the trial numbered 443 of 948
(47%) in the combination group and 315 of 960
(33%) in the ADT-alone group (Table 2). There
were 12 grade 5 adverse events, including 9 in
the combination group (2 events of pneumonia
[1 including sepsis], 2 events of stroke, and 1 event
each of dyspnea, lower respiratory tract infection,
liver failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, and chest
infection) and 3 in the ADT-alone group (2 events
of myocardial infarction and 1 event of broncho-
pneumonia). Among the 1476 patients in the
safety population in whom progression had not
occurred within the first year, the prevalence of
adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 15% in
the combination group and 11% in the ADT-
alone group. The main additional adverse events
over and above the control therapy were hyper-
tension, mild increases in aminotransferase levels,
and respiratory disorders. Further details, includ-
ing an overview according to age, are provided

(hazard ratio for treatment failure, 0.75) and
overall survival (hazard ratio for death, 0.75).
The main analysis for the comparison of combi-
nation therapy against control for survival could
be performed after the occurrence of approxi-
mately 267 deaths in the control group for 90%
power and a one-sided alpha level of 2.5%, after
we accounted for three intermediate lack-of-
benefit analyses of failure-free survival. An inde-
pendent data monitoring committee reviewed
accumulating data, guided by lack-of-benefit
stopping guidelines.
Data on patients without an event of interest
were censored when they were last known to be
event-free. The median follow-up was determined
through reversing death and censoring indica-
tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
models to estimate relative treatment effects.
These estimates were adjusted for stratification
factors (except randomizing center and ADT
method) and were stratified according to time
periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-
ization.
All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment
that they started. In the analysis of the median
duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
sored at the date of last contact with the patient
if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
Results
Patients
Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
The flow of patients through the trial is shown
in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
median follow-up was 40 months.
Treatment
The median time from randomization to the ini-
tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
median time from the initiation of ADT to the
initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
clined treatment. The median duration of abira
terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
continue through progression (51% reported per-
manent stopping for progression and 20% for
excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
report.
The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
therapy was 39% in the combination group and
40% in the ADT-alone group.
Overall Survival
There were 184 deaths in the combination group
and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
combination group, with a 3-year survival of
83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone
group (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% confi-
dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).

item.text: The outcome is a pre-specified clinical/radiologic progression composite, but the report says the trial was open-label, adds at least quarterly assessments in the combination group, and leaves further tests to physician discretion. I’m weighing those detection and judgment pathways separately from whether the endpoint itself is a valid measure.

answers.justification: The protocol prespecifies PFS as time to local progression, confirmed progression-related skeletal event, lymph-node progression, distant metastases, or prostate-cancer death; the article defines it as failure-free survival excluding biochemical failure. These clinical and radiologic events are appropriate measures of progression and death, with no evidence here that the methods are invalid or insensitive. The report does not provide a detailed validation study for each component.
unknowns: No detailed validation evidence for the individual clinical and radiologic progression components is reported.

answers.justification: Although the general schedule was every 6 weeks, then every 12 weeks, then every 6 months and annually, the report adds that combination patients were assessed at least every 3 months. It also states further tests were at treating-physician discretion and imaging was not mandated beyond baseline. This creates a plausible difference in opportunity to detect progression between groups.
unknowns: The report does not quantify how often discretionary tests or imaging were actually performed by arm.

counterevidence.implication: The common scheduled assessment sequence was broadly similar, which tempers certainty about the extent of any differential detection.

answers.justification: The comparison was explicitly open-label. Treating physicians conducted or directed assessments and discretionary tests, so relevant outcome assessors were aware of assignment.

The PFS composite includes clinical progression, and further tests were at the treating physician's discretion. Since the comparison was open-label, knowledge of allocation could affect decisions about further testing and clinical progression assessment.
unknowns: The report does not describe whether progression assessments were centrally reviewed or apply detailed blinded adjudication.

answers.justification: The open-label discretionary assessment pathway means influence was possible, but the report does not show that knowledge actually influenced PFS assessment. The composite also includes radiologic progression and prostate-cancer death, and reported event counts alone do not establish assessor influence. Thus likely influence is not supported, while the possibility remains.
unknowns: Whether knowledge of assignment affected individual clinical or radiologic progression decisions is not reported.

counterevidence.implication: The additional discretionary testing and open-label physician judgment provide a plausible pathway for influence, although no evidence establishes that it occurred.

questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish source creation/version and amendment dates from trial events and retrieval time; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An embedded SAP can be applicable evidence when its comparison, cohort, and Result fields match; an absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
The result did not follow such a pre-specified plan.
Analysis intentions or their timing are not sufficiently reported.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data; a source creation date, registry posting or update date, amendment date, or retrieval date is not automatically the relevant trial chronology.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent, and a data cutoff is not investigator unblinding. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; pre-unblinding finalization differs from ambiguous chronology only in the timing premise.

evidence.transcription: Supplementary Figure S1, “Enrolment and Randomization of Patients for the Analysis of Overall Survival.” Among 2,751 patients randomized to the trial platform, 834 were allocated to other research arms and 1,917 entered this comparison: 957 allocated to A (SOC-only) and 960 to G (SOC+AAP). Follow-up status: A, alive with data in past year n=637, alive with no data in past year n=58, died n=262; G, alive with data in past year n=718, alive with no data in past year n=58, died n=184. Efficacy analyses included 957 A and 960 G participants. The safety analysis included 960 SOC-only reported (957 A and 11 G) and 949 immediate AAP started (949 G); analyzed safety counts were 960 (4/957 A and 11 G excluded for no AE assessment) and 948 (1/949 G excluded for no AE assessment).

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

10|Interim Monitoring and Analyses
11|For each research comparison, a series of formal intermediate analyses (Activity Stages; AS) are planned
12|where activity "hurdles" are determined on an intermediate primary outcome measure (see Section 3 for
13|detail); each research arm should need to pass this in order to continue recruitment in the next part of the
14|trial. These are comparison-specific and will initially be timed according to the observed number of interim
15|events required for a formal interim analysis; beyond these activity stages data will be reviewed for each
16|comparison at regular intervals (approximately annually). These analyses will be performed by the trial team at
17|the MRC CTU at UCL.
18|The un-blinded data will be reviewed by an Independent Data Monitoring Committee (IDMC) who will advise
19|whether or not the comparison, and indeed therefore the trial, should continue on in the same way or be
20|amended. The IDMC is advisory to a Trial Steering Committee (TSC, see Protocol Section 16) which includes
21|some independent members and which is the executive body for the trial. Their roles are set out further in the
22|IDMC and TSC Charters, respectively. While a comparison is ongoing the associated accumulating data will
23|remain confidential, unless formally released by the IDMC.
24|For formal interim analyses, the IDMC will be guided by the intermediate hurdles but will make
25|recommendations based on the totality of data available to them. The IDMC will be asked to give advice on
26|whether the accumulating data from the trial justifies continuing recruitment of further patients or further
27|follow-up; the guidelines for discontinuation of accrual for interim Activity Stages, together with results from
28|any other trials relevant to the comparison will be used by the IDMC in this decision process. Where the sample
29|size for a comparison is pre-specified, and as such recruitment may have completed prior to a formal
30|intermediate analysis, any recommendations from the IDMC will consider the continuation of treatment only, as
31|opposed to the continuation of recruitment, and make recommendations to the TSC appropriately. Where a
32|decision is made to continue, the IDMC will advise on the frequency of future reviews of the data on the basis
33|of accrual (if the comparison is still recruiting) and event rates.

10|Main Analysis
11|For each research comparison that continues (recruitment) into the final Efficacy Stage (ES), the final analysis
12|will be triggered by a pre-specified number of definitive primary outcome events being reported for the
13|relevant patients on the control arm of that comparison; indeed having 96% of such events would be
14|considered sufficient to trigger this final analysis.
15|7.8
16|Factorial Thoughts
17|7.8.1 Factorial Analysis (Pre-specified)
18|Analysis of the original arms B, C and E, and also the celecoxib-containing arms, as a factorial design will be
19|reported as a secondary analysis using a model containing both main effects. The analysis took the form of one
20|Cox PH model including both the main treatment effects. Simulations may be carried out to assess the power
21|to detect the presence of a treatment interaction in a further exploratory model with both main effects and an
22|interaction term. The prior discussions around this type of analysis can be found in the document
23|"Factorial_Analysis_Notes_2014_05_06_v1.pdf13".
24|Survival data for those other research arms which were initiated at the same time will be reported at this point.
25|7.9
26|Statistical Methods
27|Full details of all planned analyses are reported in Section 8.
28|7.9.1 Time-to-event analyses
29|Time-to-event data will be presented using Kaplan-Meier plots. In all time-to-event analyses, patients that have
30|not experienced the event in question (e.g. progression, death) censor date will be used, as defined in Section
31|5. For KM plots all patients randomised to the comparison being analysed will be included. Those patients, who
32|have no reported event and contribute no information, such that they are censored at the date of
33|randomisation, will be censored with a time of 0.1 days.
34|The HR will be taken from a Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for those stratification factors used at
35|randomisation (see Section 5) except for centre and method of hormones, and stratified by the relevant time
36|period/strata for when the comparison was recruiting (see Section 7.3).
37|Differences in time-to-event outcomes will be assessed using the log-rank c2 test and expressed using a hazard
38|ratio (HR) with both a 1-sided 90% confidence interval and also a 2-sided 95% confidence interval; where the
39|design alpha differs from 0.025 the upper limit of corresponding relevant 1-sided confidence interval will be
40|presented (for example, for an alpha of 0.25 this would be the upper limit of a 1-sided 75% confidence
41|interval). The number of events observed and the log-rank expected number of events will be presented.

9|Alternative estimation of the treatment effect will use exploratory methods e.g. log-rank hazard ratio. Flexible
10|parametric models, modelling the difference between treatment groups over time, will be fitted to the
11|time-to-event data with and without including time-dependent treatment effects.
12|7.9.2 Proportional and Non-Proportional hazards
13|The assumption of proportional-hazards (PH) will be tested on the basis of Schoenfeld residuals after fitting the
14|cox model. Application in Stata will be using the command -estat phtest-. Appropriate methods will be applied
15|to the data in the case of any violation, and presented alongside the primary analysis to aid interpretation; see
16|details below.
17|If there is no evidence of non-PH in the treatment effect, the HR for the adjusted Cox model takes primacy.
18|If there is evidence of non-PH in the treatment effect, the HRs are difficult to interpret and the restricted mean
19|survival time14 (RMST) constructed from a flexible parametric model with time-varying treatment effects will
20|take primacy. This analysis will use a flexible parametric model, adjusted for the stratification factors used at
21|randomisation (except for centre and method of hormones) and relevant time strata, to determine the time-
22|dependent treatment effect and then predict values needed for subsequent RMST analysis. The application of
23|this methodology will be particularly useful in the case where there is adequate evidence that the proportional
24|hazard assumptions are violated at the 5% level (i.e. P<0.05). Application in Stata will be using the command
25|-strmst-.
26|RMST will be calculated and reported for the main treatment effects regardless of whether the PH assumption
27|is violated, as this is recognised as a useful measure. The time within which RMST will be computed will be
28|determined by the timing of events in the control arm (using the command - maturity_rmst- in Stata). For this
29|purpose, t* (the time up to when we want to compute the outcome measure) will be defined as the maximum
30|available follow-up time if clinically meaningful, where there is most power for the analysis, or a suitable salient
31|time point otherwise, for each research comparison.
32|For formal intermediate analyses, the level of confidence around the HR will be noted; the same level
33|confidence interval as for that stage will be constructed around the difference in RMST with the appropriate
34|confidence interval level determined according to the alpha calculated for that intermediate analysis. If the
35|lower bound of this confidence interval includes zero (no difference) the research arm will be considered
36|insufficiently active.

38|Analysis of those outcomes where there are considered to be competing risks will be done in addition to an
39|adjusted Cox model with a competing risk defined as any event the patient would likely have experienced had
40|they not experienced the outcome of interest first.

considerations: Use the review's prespecified outcome-domain eligibility criteria, not only the reported Result, and compare the reported measurement with all eligible alternatives. An applicable plan's correspondence and chronology are relevant context but do not themselves establish results-driven selection. The approved Result fixes the target being assessed; it does not erase other eligible measurements in the outcome domain or make their selection an observed fact.

Abiraterone for Prostate Cancer
ards (P = 0.31) or of heterogeneity of the treat-
ment effect according to metastatic status at
randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
parisons in patients without metastatic disease
at randomization are immature, currently with
78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
groups (Fig. 2A).
Failure-free Survival
There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
survival was 75% in the combination group and
45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
the combination group and 30.0 months in the
ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
progression or death from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
80% in the combination group and 62% in the
ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
radiologic progression or death from prostate
cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
mentary Appendix). This difference was most
marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
Exploratory Analyses
Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
noted in older patients. In patients younger than
70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
there were 65 events in the combination group
and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
0.50; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.68; P = 0.10 for interac-
tion). In patients younger than 70 years of age,
there were 93 deaths from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 154 in the ADT-alone
group (subhazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39 to
0.66); in patients 70 years of age or older, there
were 47 deaths from prostate cancer in the com-
bination group and 62 in the ADT-alone group
(subhazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.17;
P = 0.08 for interaction).
Adverse Events
Patients in the safety population who reported
adverse events of grade 3 or higher during their
entire time in the trial numbered 443 of 948
(47%) in the combination group and 315 of 960
(33%) in the ADT-alone group (Table 2). There
were 12 grade 5 adverse events, including 9 in
the combination group (2 events of pneumonia
[1 including sepsis], 2 events of stroke, and 1 event
each of dyspnea, lower respiratory tract infection,
liver failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, and chest
infection) and 3 in the ADT-alone group (2 events
of myocardial infarction and 1 event of broncho-
pneumonia). Among the 1476 patients in the
safety population in whom progression had not
occurred within the first year, the prevalence of
adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 15% in
the combination group and 11% in the ADT-
alone group. The main additional adverse events
over and above the control therapy were hyper-
tension, mild increases in aminotransferase levels,
and respiratory disorders. Further details, includ-
ing an overview according to age, are provided

ADT-alone group for both failure-free survival
(hazard ratio for treatment failure, 0.75) and
overall survival (hazard ratio for death, 0.75).
The main analysis for the comparison of combi-
nation therapy against control for survival could
be performed after the occurrence of approxi-
mately 267 deaths in the control group for 90%
power and a one-sided alpha level of 2.5%, after
we accounted for three intermediate lack-of-
benefit analyses of failure-free survival. An inde-
pendent data monitoring committee reviewed
accumulating data, guided by lack-of-benefit
stopping guidelines.
Data on patients without an event of interest
were censored when they were last known to be
event-free. The median follow-up was determined
through reversing death and censoring indica-
tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
models to estimate relative treatment effects.
These estimates were adjusted for stratification
factors (except randomizing center and ADT
method) and were stratified according to time
periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-
ization.
All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment
that they started. In the analysis of the median
duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
sored at the date of last contact with the patient
if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
Results
Patients
Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
The flow of patients through the trial is shown
in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
median follow-up was 40 months.
Treatment
The median time from randomization to the ini-
tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
median time from the initiation of ADT to the
initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
clined treatment. The median duration of abira
terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
continue through progression (51% reported per-
manent stopping for progression and 20% for
excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
report.
The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
therapy was 39% in the combination group and
40% in the ADT-alone group.
Overall Survival
There were 184 deaths in the combination group
and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
combination group, with a 3-year survival of
83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone
group (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% confi-
dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).

Statistical Methods
Full details of all planned analyses are reported in Section 8.
7.9.1 Time-to-event analyses
Time-to-event data will be presented using Kaplan-Meier plots. In all time-to-event analyses, patients that have
not experienced the event in question (e.g. progression, death) censor date will be used, as defined in Section
5. For KM plots all patients randomised to the comparison being analysed will be included. Those patients, who
have no reported event and contribute no information, such that they are censored at the date of
randomisation, will be censored with a time of 0.1 days.
The HR will be taken from a Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for those stratification factors used at
randomisation (see Section 5) except for centre and method of hormones, and stratified by the relevant time
period/strata for when the comparison was recruiting (see Section 7.3).
Differences in time-to-event outcomes will be assessed using the log-rank c2 test and expressed using a hazard
ratio (HR) with both a 1-sided 90% confidence interval and also a 2-sided 95% confidence interval; where the
design alpha differs from 0.025 the upper limit of corresponding relevant 1-sided confidence interval will be
presented (for example, for an alpha of 0.25 this would be the upper limit of a 1-sided 75% confidence
interval). The number of events observed and the log-rank expected number of events will be presented.

30|7.12.1 Data linkage for death
31|Data from ONS or similar sources will be used, when and/or where available, to confirm deaths, detect
32|unreported deaths and determine cause of death (if unknown and/or unreported). Where such external data
33|sources are used for analyses of survival or disease-specific survival, patients who are not confirmed by this
34|data source as having died will be censored close to the time of receipt of this external data; the exact time will
35|be determined in discussion with the provider of such data and will be reported explicitly. For example, for two
36|previous CTU-led trials in prostate cancer, survival data were available from ONS and, in discussion with the
37|ONS Chief Statistician, it was reasonable to assume that patients were still alive 8 weeks before data transfer if
38|they were not reported as having died. This approach accepted that deaths referred to a coroner for review
39|would have been inappropriately classified as censored rather than dead (with the time of censoring possibly
40|later than the actual time of death).

9|7.13 Populations
10|We define two populations for analysis; the intention-to-treat population and the safety population.
11|1. Intention-to-treat (ITT) population
12|- Comprised of all randomised patients, whether or not they actually received the allocated trial
13|treatment.
14|- In ITT analyses by treatment arm, patients will be included in the treatment arm to which they were
15|randomised.
16|2. Safety population
17|- Comprised of patients who have been administered at least one dose of their allocated trial
18|treatment.
19|- Patients will be classed as having started trial treatment if they report a treatment start date, report
20|an SAE which is treatment related, or report death as being within 4 weeks of trial treatment (&
21|related to trial treatment)
22|- In safety population analyses, patients will be included in the treatment arm corresponding to the
23|treatment they actually started; for example an Arm B patient not starting zoledronic acid will be
24|included with Arm A patients, whilst an Arm E patient not starting docetaxel but starting zoledronic
25|acid will be included with Arm B patients.
26|- Two sensitivity safety analyses will be conducted around this classification, wherein patients with
27|unclear treatment starting status will be included firstly in allocated treatment arm (making the
28|assumption they start trial treatment) and secondly in the control arm (making the assumption they
29|don't start trial treatment).
30|The ITT population will be included in all analyses unless specified. The safety population will be included in
31|analyses of adverse events and other safety data (safety analyses).
32|For visual illustration a CONSORT flow diagram will clearly identify any patients found to be ineligible
33|post-randomisation or stopping trial follow-up early; these patients will be included in relevant analyses where
34|possible. For reference, a template flow diagram can be found in S:\Stampede_Stats\SAP.

9|7.14 Safety Analyses
10|Safety analyses will be performed and presented on the safety population; for headline numbers reporting
11|toxicity, these will be repeated on the ITT population as defined in Section 7.13.
12|All safety analyses will focus on adverse events experienced during treatment and up to 30 days after the end
13|of treatment (see Protocol section 11.2.1.D).
14|Safety will be evaluated by tabulation of adverse events at or up to pre-defined follow-up time points. Adverse
15|events will be classified using the NCI Common Toxicity Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE v3.0; updated to
16|CTCAE v4.0 for all assessments dated from Protocol v15.0 (05-Sep-2016) onwards) and summarised for each
17|treatment arm. Reported grading is "0 = toxicity not experienced" up to "5 = fatal".
18|Adverse events (AEs) may be detected through several sources:
19|1. Follow-up CRF - routinely reported symptoms and "toxicities" (severity not seriousness)
20|·
21|AEs reported here up to Sep-2016.
22|2. Toxicity CRF
23|- routinely reported symptoms and "toxicities" (severity not seriousness)
24|·
25|AEs reported here from Sep-2016 onwards.
26|·
27|Linked to routine follow-up visits, treatment actions and permanent stopping of treatment.
28|3. SAE CRF
29|- spontaneously reported serious adverse events (severity and seriousness)
30|Not all serious events are severe and vice versa. "Seriousness" is a term specific to the reporting of events to
31|regulatory bodies. We have prioritised the consideration of "severity" for balancing against activity data. SAE
32|forms and follow-up forms both request the severity of events. Therefore, these sources can be merged to
33|form one dataset for reporting "severe" data. The focus will be on toxicities with grade 3, 4 or 5 (fatal),
34|however all toxicity grades will be reported for completeness.
35|For toxicity data reported at set time points from randomisation this will be reported only for patients who
36|have not progressed by the set time point; this is because for patients on either the control arm or research
37|arms where trial treatment is to be stopped at progression toxicity data is only expected up to the time of first
38|reported progression. For patients on research arms where trial treatment can continue beyond first
39|progression (namely current Arms G, J and K), an additional report of toxicity data at specific time points from
40|randomisation will be presented only for research arm patients still on treatment at that time. Reporting
41|windows will be defined around any such set time points which will be as close to the time of interest whilst
42|accepting that clinical practice means that most patients will not be reviewed on a specific day.
43|For toxicity data reported up to pre-specified time points from randomisation this will include all patients
44|with follow-up/toxicity/SAE data available within that time frame.
45|All patients receive ADT as standard-of-care and so interest will be in the 'additional toxicity reported' for
46|patients on research arm relative to control arm, compared informally. Interest will also be in any proportion of
47|known treatment toxicity viewed to be above that which is expected in this population.

9|7.15 Missing Data
10|Missing data will be assumed to be missing completely at random (MCAR) in intention-to-treat analyses;
11|exploratory analyses may be undertaken to further understand any missing data.
12|7.16 Pre-specified Subgroup Effects
13|STAMPEDE recruits patients at high risk of dying from prostate cancer and who are starting long-term hormone
14|therapy for the first time (hormone-naïve disease). This is a broad spectrum of patients including both men
15|with metastases at randomisation and men without metastases, and men with de novo disease or disease
16|relapsing after previous local therapy.
17|7.16.1 Stratification Factors
18|The stratification factors considered at the point of randomisation will form subgroups in which to assess
19|treatment effect, with an interaction p-value of less than 0.1 used to suggest evidence of a difference across
20|the relevant subgroups; as with all subgroups it is accepted that there is limited power both for the interaction
21|and within group analysis. In addition the time periods the relevant comparison was recruiting across (see
22|Table 5) and also whether the patient entered the trial with recurrent disease will be considered as subgroups
23|in which to assess treatment effect, along with pre-hormone therapy PSA as a continuous variable.
24|7.16.2 Metastatic status
25|For all research comparisons where both metastatic and non-metastatic patients are eligible metastatic status
26|at randomisation will be a pre-specified subgroup. In such instances the non-metastatic patients are a smaller
27|subset of patients within STAMPEDE and their event rate is lower, so the TMG accepts that there will be limited
28|power to make reliable comment on those patients. Tests for heterogeneity by metastatic status will be

Randomization and Masking
Randomization was performed centrally by tele-
phone with the use of a computerized algorithm,
which was developed and maintained by the MRC
Clinical Trials Unit at UCL. Minimization with a
random element of 80% was used, with stratifi-
cation according to randomizing center, age at
randomization (<70 vs. ≥70 years), the presence
or absence of metastases, planned use of pros-
tate radiotherapy (yes vs. no), nodal involvement
(negative vs. indeterminate vs. positive), World
Health Organization performance status (0 vs.
1 or 2 [on a scale of 0 to 4, with higher numbers
indicating greater disability]), type of ADT, and
regular, long-term use of aspirin or nonsteroidal
antiinflammatory drugs (yes vs. no). The assign-
ment ratio was 1:1 to standard of care alone or
with abiraterone acetate and prednisolone (combi-
nation therapy). The comparison was open-label,
because masking of the treatment assignment
was deemed impracticable. Eligible patients could
be assigned to any of the trial groups that were
open; we focus here on patients assigned con-
temporaneously to ADT alone or with abiraterone
and prednisolone.

Data on patients without an event of interest
were censored when they were last known to be
event-free. The median follow-up was determined
through reversing death and censoring indica-
tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
models to estimate relative treatment effects.
These estimates were adjusted for stratification
factors (except randomizing center and ADT
method) and were stratified according to time
periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-

parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-
ization.
All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment

ment effect according to metastatic status at
randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
parisons in patients without metastatic disease
at randomization are immature, currently with
78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
groups (Fig. 2A).
Failure-free Survival
There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
survival was 75% in the combination group and
45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
the combination group and 30.0 months in the
ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
progression or death from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
80% in the combination group and 62% in the
ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
radiologic progression or death from prostate
cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
mentary Appendix). This difference was most
marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
Exploratory Analyses
Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
noted in older patients. In patients younger than
70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
there were 65 events in the combination group
and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,

7.12.1 Data linkage for death
Data from ONS or similar sources will be used, when and/or where available, to confirm deaths, detect
unreported deaths and determine cause of death (if unknown and/or unreported). Where such external data
sources are used for analyses of survival or disease-specific survival, patients who are not confirmed by this
data source as having died will be censored close to the time of receipt of this external data; the exact time will
be determined in discussion with the provider of such data and will be reported explicitly. For example, for two
previous CTU-led trials in prostate cancer, survival data were available from ONS and, in discussion with the
ONS Chief Statistician, it was reasonable to assume that patients were still alive 8 weeks before data transfer if
they were not reported as having died. This approach accepted that deaths referred to a coroner for review
would have been inappropriately classified as censored rather than dead (with the time of censoring possibly
later than the actual time of death).
A sensitivity analysis for linked deaths will be performed excluding those events and censoring at last contact
as being event-free.

Statistical Methods
Full details of all planned analyses are reported in Section 8.
7.9.1 Time-to-event analyses
Time-to-event data will be presented using Kaplan-Meier plots. In all time-to-event analyses, patients that have
not experienced the event in question (e.g. progression, death) censor date will be used, as defined in Section
5. For KM plots all patients randomised to the comparison being analysed will be included. Those patients, who
have no reported event and contribute no information, such that they are censored at the date of
randomisation, will be censored with a time of 0.1 days.
The HR will be taken from a Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for those stratification factors used at
randomisation (see Section 5) except for centre and method of hormones, and stratified by the relevant time
period/strata for when the comparison was recruiting (see Section 7.3).
Differences in time-to-event outcomes will be assessed using the log-rank c2 test and expressed using a hazard
ratio (HR) with both a 1-sided 90% confidence interval and also a 2-sided 95% confidence interval; where the
design alpha differs from 0.025 the upper limit of corresponding relevant 1-sided confidence interval will be
presented (for example, for an alpha of 0.25 this would be the upper limit of a 1-sided 75% confidence
interval). The number of events observed and the log-rank expected number of events will be presented.
